title: Looped boat propellers could help quiet the ocean for whales
summary:
Whales use sound to find food and communicate. In quiet water, they can hear one another’s calls from hundreds of miles away. But the ocean also carries noise from ships and other human activities.

Some shipping noise overlaps with the low sounds whales use. That can make important calls harder to hear.

One source of boat noise is the propeller, the spinning part that pushes a boat through water. Fast-moving propellers can create tiny bubbles that collapse and release sharp bursts of sound. This process is called cavitation.

A Detroit company, Sharrow Marine, has designed a different propeller. Instead of blades with open tips, its blades form twisting loops. The company says this reduces swirling water near the tips and creates less cavitation.

Sharrow reports that independent tests found reductions of up to seven decibels in underwater noise within the sound range whales use to communicate. Decibels measure sound levels. The amount of noise reduction can vary with the sound’s pitch and how the equipment is used.

The company is now working with Ocean Alliance to test the propellers on research trips near whales. It is still early, so quieter measurements do not yet prove better lives for the animals.

The idea began with a different puzzle. Founder Greg Sharrow wanted to film a violinist using a drone without its loud buzzing. Thinking about quieter blades led him from flying machines to boats—and a possible way to make the ocean easier to hear.
why_it_matters: Whales rely on sound. Testing quieter propellers could help researchers learn whether changing boat equipment reduces interference with whale communication.
